newsitem.title: POLAND: Romania seeks Polish cooperation on Europe road.
newsitem.headline: Romania seeks Polish cooperation on Europe road.

text.p: Romanian President Emil Constantinescu said on Tuesday his country and Poland could move faster towards their goal of European integration if they worked together more.
"Our haste towards Europe after the fall of totalitarianism has meant we paid less attention to each other," he told the foreign affairs committees of both houses of parliament.

Constantinescu -- a reformer who chose Poland for his first official foreign trip since his election in November last year, when he defeated ex-communist Ion Iliescu -- said countries set on joining west European structures had seen this as a contest.
"Now it is becoming ever clearer that integration is not an independent effort, but a road travelled jointly," he said, appealing for Polish-Romanian solidarity.
Constantinescu said any formal Polish-Romanian joint entry into the EU was not on the cards.

"But it seems to me the process of integration could be quicker and less burdensome if our governments proposed -- alongside legal and economic conditions required by integration -- the achievement of some harmony or...synergy in aims and means," he said.

Constantinescu suggested new cooperation could flourish in the framework of the Central European Initiative, which Romania joined last year, and the Black Sea Economic Cooperation forum, on which Poland has observer status.

He said bilateral trade would be greatly eased by Romania's admission into the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA), a goal which Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski backed on Monday, the first day of Constantinescu's visit.
CEFTA now groups the Czech Republic, Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and Slovenia.

Like Poland, Romania seeks to join the European Union and NATO and would like to be admitted to the defence alliance in 1999, in the first wave of new members, which are widely expected to be Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary.

Senior Polish opposition politician and foreign affairs specialist Janusz Onyszkiewicz said a key message of Constantinescu's trip, due to end on Wednesday morning, had been Romania's desire to be among the first in NATO.
"Romania realises the governments of Mr Iliescu and of the circles from which he emerged were times lost for Romania. Whether it can catch up, I don't know," said Onyszkiewicz.
